1:
Ellicott explains the delay. In the first tumult of his joy Jacob had determined on hastening to Egypt, but second thoughts made him hesitate. He would call to mind the boding prophecy that Abraham's seed should be enslaved in a foreign land. It might even be a sin, involving the loss of the covenant, to quit Canaan at all. Abraham had expressly forbidden Isaac to abandon it, and Isaac himself had been commanded to stay when he thought of going down. So Jacob resolved to consult God first, and no place could be fitter than Beersheba, where both Abraham and Isaac had built altars and which lay on the road from Hebron into Egypt.

Calvin weighs the cost. Jacob was about to lose the sight of the land that was the type and pledge of the heavenly country. Might it not come into his mind that he had been deluded all along with a vain hope? By renewing the memory of the covenant he applies a remedy against falling from the faith. He offers on the very boundary of the land, to testify that in leaving the country he does not leave the God in whose worship he was educated. Henry and Wesley account for the sacrifices three ways. They were thanksgiving for the blessed change in his family. They were petition for God's presence on the journey. And they were consultation, for the heathen enquired of their oracles by sacrifice, and Jacob would not stir until he had asked God's leave.

The answer came the next night. Calvin notes that the vision gave dignity to the oracle, but insists that a silent vision would have profited nothing. Superstition eagerly snatches at mere spectres; no living image of God can exist without the word, which follows the vision as if it were its soul. Henry hears the old name in the double call, Jacob, Jacob, meant to remind him of his low estate, since his present fears scarcely became an Israel.

Henry and Wesley set out what Jacob had been afraid of. He was a hundred and thirty, and the old are afraid of that which is high. He feared his sons would be tainted with the idolatry of Egypt and forget the God of their fathers. He could not think of laying his bones in Egypt. Clarke answers each from the promise: he may go down safely, the covenant will be kept even there, God will bring his bones back, and Joseph will do him the last kind office. He and Calvin both explain the closing of the eyes as the duty of the nearest in blood, though Calvin admits the wish showed some infirmity of the flesh, which God indulged to soften the grief of a fresh banishment.

Calvin hears new vigour in the words rose up. Henry watches how the old man travelled: not in a chariot, though his own son rode in one, but in a waggon, for Jacob affected nothing stately. He took his cattle and goods so as not to be beholden to Pharaoh, and so that it might never be said they came beggars into Egypt. Gill rejects Jarchi's guess that Jacob had signed over all he gained in Padan-aram to Esau for his share in the cave of Machpelah. Both Calvin and Keil turn to the painted tomb at Beni-hassan, where strangers arrive in Egypt with their goods on asses and two children in panniers. Wesley closes with the arithmetic. Sixty-six went down, and with Joseph, his two sons, and Jacob himself the house came to seventy. It was two hundred and fifteen years since the promise of a great nation, and the branch that carried it had grown only to seventy, so that the multiplying of those seventy in Egypt might appear the more illustrious.
8:
Ellicott treats the list as a legal document rather than a family record. To Israel taking possession of Canaan it would be of the highest importance, being as it were their title-deed to the land, and it is drawn up accordingly. Men really grandsons are entered as sons, having taken the place of sons as heads of families. All are represented as born in Canaan, not in a natural sense but as the rightful heirs of the country. Technically every head of a family was born there, so no objection could be raised against one actually born in Egypt. Gill reads the opening phrase the same way: the children of Israel here are not precisely Jacob's offspring but the body of the people as they stood on the day they went down, Jacob included.

The dates are where Ellicott presses hardest. Pharez was an infant when carried down, and it is difficult enough to find room for his birth between the return from Padan-aram and the descent; for his two sons there is no space whatsoever. Benjamin is given ten sons, though he was at most about thirty when he went into Egypt, and some of the ten are called his grandsons elsewhere. Commentators have tried to make Benjamin older, but only by upsetting conclusions they had reached themselves. Nothing, Ellicott says, so legitimately produces scepticism as facts marshalled to suit the passage in hand and irreconcilable with the difficulties already met. Clarke offers the standard relief: some names are brought in by anticipation, the persons being born during the seventeen years Jacob afterwards spent in Egypt, so that the going down includes those years. The variation of names elsewhere, Jemuel for Nemuel or Jachin for Jarib, he thinks no great matter, since one man commonly bore two.

The harder question is the total. Moses gives seventy and Stephen gives seventy-five. Calvin lays the difference to the transcribers. He rejects Augustine's solution, that Stephen counted three born later in Egypt, for then the catalogue must have run far longer. The corruption crept into one Greek passage only, and when numerals were written as marks a single letter was easily displaced. Clarke traces the same five to the Septuagint, which adds descendants of Manasseh and Ephraim at the naming of Joseph's sons. He prefers Hales's reckoning, which needs no addition to the text. The sixty-six leave out the sons' wives, of whom nine were living, Judah's and Simeon's being dead and Joseph's already in Egypt; sixty-six and nine make Stephen's seventy-five, the true force of all his kindred. Ellicott states the Hebrew arithmetic plainly: sixty-six leaves out Jacob, Joseph and Joseph's two sons, and seventy counts them in.

Calvin lingers over the oddities. Moses names the mother of Shaul alone, which Calvin takes for a mark of dishonour on his race, the fathers being on their guard against mixing with a nation heaven had separated from them. Ellicott passes on the Jewish tradition instead, that Shaul was really Dinah's son by Shechem, adopted by Simeon to save his sister's honour. Where Leah's sons are summed at thirty-three and only thirty-two are named, Calvin reckons Jacob himself as the first, and rejects as overstrained the rabbinic guess that Jochebed is meant. Ellicott explains why the later lists disagree: spellings vary, and names drop out once a family has no representative left. The confusion in Benjamin's line he lays to the ruinous war of Judges, after which the tribe repaired its records with the utmost care, so that the pedigree in Chronicles is the royal line of Saul. Calvin draws the moral from the smallness of the number. The more improbable it looks that seventy should become such a multitude, the more clearly does the grace of God shine out of so dry a fountain.
28:
Judah goes ahead, and the commentators agree why. Gill notes he stood higher in his father's esteem than Reuben, Simeon and Levi, who had displeased him, and had endeared himself to Joseph by his speech in the hall. Clarke calls him a man of sense and eloquent. Keil and Delitzsch explain the errand: he was to get Joseph's instructions about where they should settle, then guide the company into Goshen. Henry reads the courtesy as owing to the government under whose protection these strangers were coming, and warns against giving offence to any, and least of all to the higher powers. Calvin adds what Jacob was actually asking: not that a house be built for him, but only that he might pitch his tent without molestation. Some unoccupied place had to be assigned, lest by taking the pastures of the inhabitants he give occasion for a tumult.

Ellicott explains why Goshen and not Egypt proper. In the narrow and populous Nile valley they could not have kept an isolated life, and isolation was indispensable if they were to grow into a nation fit to guard a growing revelation. Since the Egyptians farmed and hated shepherds, Israel ran no risk of being absorbed so long as they kept their old pursuits, and there they would remain as distinct from the rest of mankind as they had been in Canaan. Clarke reports that the Septuagint calls it the land of Rameses, and that Goshen was Heroopolis, the city of heroes, still known by that name in the days of Josephus.

The meeting itself is handled with unusual care. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the word for showing himself is one generally used only of the appearance of God, chosen to mark the glory in which Joseph came out to meet his father. Ellicott raises the question who fell on whose neck. Most versions take it of Joseph, but Maimonides held that a son would not take so great a liberty with his father, and our translation, which understands it of Jacob, gives the most natural sense. Henry measures the weeping against an earlier scene. Joseph had wept on Benjamin's neck, but on his father's he wept a good while; the brother was dear, the father dearer. He notes how near sorrow and joy stand in this world, when the same tears serve for both, and that in heaven there is perfect joy but no tears of joy. Calvin uses the scene to show that the holy Fathers were not destitute of natural affection, adding only that such affections always exceed their bounds, and so need not to be rooted out but kept within them.

Then the old man says he can die. Henry and Wesley refuse to read this as weariness of life. It was still desirable to live with Joseph and see his honour, but the first meeting gave him more satisfaction than he thought fit to ask of this world. Henry observes that Jacob lived seventeen years after wishing to die at once, and that death will not come just when we call for it. Ellicott says he will wait for it calmly now the great longing of his soul is satisfied, and Clarke wonders whether old Simeon had this place in view when he asked to depart in peace. Joseph meanwhile plans. Henry marks the reversal in it: they had once contrived to be rid of him, and he now contrives to settle them, which is rendering good for evil. Calvin defends him against the charge of craft, since the richness of Goshen was perfectly well known to Pharaoh, who had offered them the best of the land unasked. And he finds the contempt of the Egyptians profitable. Mingled with them, Israel might have been scattered; loathed by them, they learned to cherish their union, and the body of the Church was not dispersed.
33:
Gill explains why the answer had to be so exact. Joseph told his brothers to be particular about their occupation so that it might direct Pharaoh how to dispose of them. Goshen abounded in good pasture and was the fittest place for them. It also lay near enough for Joseph to reach, since he may have lived at On, to whose province Goshen belonged. It was the nearest part of the land to Canaan, so that they might the sooner get away when occasion came. And it kept them out of the heart of the country. Gill glosses the trade itself as breeding, feeding and selling cattle, an employment they had never left, and one Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had followed before them. Clarke describes the ground on Bruce's authority. Goshen lay east of the Nile and was never overflowed by it, bounded by the mountains of the Thebaid on the south, the Nile and the Mediterranean on the west and north, and the Red Sea and the Arabian desert on the east. Its proper name was Geshen, the country of grass or pasturage, in contrast to the rest of the land, which was sown after the flood had gone down.

Why every shepherd should be an abomination is the question of the verse, since the Egyptians kept cattle themselves and Pharaoh had his own herds. Clarke offers three reasons. Shepherds and feeders of cattle were commonly a sort of lawless freebooting bandits, making inroads on villages and carrying off whatever spoils they could find. Then there were the king-shepherds of Manetho, marauders out of Arabia and Syria who subdued Egypt and ruled it with great tyranny for two hundred and fifty-nine years, whose name was execrated long after they had been driven out. But the best reason, he thinks, is that men like the Israelites sacrificed the very animals the Egyptians held sacred, the ox above all; and he cites the Roman historian, who says the Jews kill the ram to insult Jupiter Ammon and the ox which Egypt worships under the name of Apis. Ellicott takes the clause for a remark of the narrator, and finds it confirmed by the monuments, where shepherds are drawn unshaven and ill-dressed. He supposes the Egyptian peasantry left their beasts to the women and children while the men worked the fields. As for the dislike, he doubts the Hyksos are the explanation, since their conquest was possibly later than Joseph. Men who live settled lives always dislike wandering clans whose cattle prey on enclosed land, and who are not scrupulous about rights of property; and Egypt had perpetual war with the Hittites and raids from Semitic tribes on its eastern frontier.

Both writers see what the contempt was worth. Ellicott observes that in an arable valley the cattle kept would be only such as farming needed, whereas cattle were the whole wealth of Israel. Clarke says the scheme succeeded, and that the preservation of their religion and of their lives followed from it, though some of their posterity corrupted themselves later. He closes with Warburton. The promise of Canaan could not be performed until the family was strong enough to take and keep the land, so they had to live among idolaters and live unmixed; and whoever examines their history sees that the Israelites had a violent propensity to join themselves to Gentile nations and practise their manners. Egypt was the one country where they could stay so long and not be confounded with the natives, its people being forbidden fellowship with strangers and bearing besides a particular aversion to the trade of shepherds. What looked like an insult was the wall that kept them a people.
